articles.title: Russia claims strikes on Starlink terminals, drone sites in Ukraine's Sumy
articles.summary: Russia's military struck drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine's Sumy region, while a separate overnight
articles.body: Russia's military struck drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine's Sumy region, while a separate overnight attack on Zaporizhzhia injured 11 people, according to Ukrainian and Russian officials.The Russian defence ministry said its forces had hit the military targets in Sumy, Interfax news agency reported on Tuesday.In Zaporizhzhia, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said 11 people were injured in the Russian attack, with a woman in serious condition. He warned that people could be trapped under the rubble after strikes damaged apartment buildings, private homes, transport infrastructure and cars.Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia was preparing further attacks and urged people to pay attention to air raid alerts.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's intelligence had indicated that Russia was preparing new strikes. He also called on the United States and other countries supplying anti-ballistic missile interceptors to Ukraine to take the warnings seriously."Every Patriot missile we have is a blow to Russia – a blow to its contempt for diplomacy and for life,"Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine needed more missiles for its Patriot air defence systems.He said the war continued because Russia believed it could "kill and destroy", and urged Washington to take the necessary decisions to provide Ukraine with additional interceptors to protect its cities and infrastructure.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Welsh slate museum housed in historic quarry workshops closed in 2024 for a major renovation; a fresh £2.4 million government grant will help restore the UNESCO-listed industrial site and create new facilities
articles.summary: There are places where history is not simply preserved in books, photographs or museum displays, but remains embedded in the very buildings where it
articles.body: There are places where history is not simply preserved in books, photographs or museum displays, but remains embedded in the very buildings where it unfolded. Old workshops, factories and industrial sites often hold traces of an era when their machinery was part of everyday life, and the people who worked there helped shape the fortunes of entire regions. With time, however, the industries that once kept these places alive may disappear, leaving behind structures that offer a glimpse into the skills, labour and communities of an earlier age. Preserving them is not merely an exercise in restoring old buildings; it is also about ensuring that the stories associated with them are not lost.In north-west Wales, the National Slate Museum in Llanberis is one such place. Housed in the historic Gilfach Ddu workshops of the former Dinorwig quarry, the museum preserves the legacy of an industry that transformed the region and became an important part of its cultural identity. The site, which forms part of the UNESCO-listed Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales, closed to visitors in November 2024 for a major redevelopment. Now, a fresh £2.4 million investment from the Welsh Government is expected to support the restoration of its historic buildings and the creation of new facilities as the museum prepares for its eventual reopening.According to the Welsh Government's announcement, the funding will go towards the next phase of a wider redevelopment project being carried out by Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales. Culture and Sport Cabinet Minister Heledd Fychan confirmed the additional investment during a visit to the site, highlighting the importance of preserving the historic workshops while making the museum more welcoming and accessible to future visitors. The project brings together conservation work and the development of new facilities, with the aim of giving the museum a sustainable future without compromising its industrial character.What the restoration work at the museum involvesA major part of the restoration involves bringing the historic workshops back to life while retaining the features that make them an important part of Wales' industrial heritage. The work is not simply about repairing an old building, but about preserving the details that have survived from the days when the workshops served the Dinorwig quarry. This includes the restoration of 113 original windows, which together contain almost 12,000 individual pieces of glass. Rather than replacing them altogether, specialists are carefully repairing the existing frames and glass panels wherever possible. The original wooden doors are also being restored, with damaged sections of timber repaired to retain their historic appearance.Alongside the conservation work, the redevelopment is also preparing the museum for a different kind of visitor experience. The plans include improved spaces and facilities that will allow people to explore the history of the slate industry while spending more time at the site. The challenge is to strike a balance between preserving a place that reflects a very different period of industrial life and making it suitable for visitors today. In that sense, the restoration is as much about protecting the museum's original character as it is about preparing it for the future.What new facilities visitors can expect after reopeningAmong the additions planned for the museum is a new café, learning and community centre, which will replace the older shop and café buildings that were demolished during the redevelopment. The new space will give visitors somewhere to spend time at the site, while also providing facilities for school visits, educational activities and local community events. A dedicated play area is also being developed for children, with elements inspired by the region's slate heritage. Along with improved exhibition spaces, these facilities are expected to make the museum more accessible to families and younger visitors, giving them an opportunity to learn about the industry beyond the machinery and objects on display.The National Slate Museum's redevelopment comes at a time when preserving industrial heritage has become an important part of keeping local histories alive. The slate industry may no longer define everyday life in north-west Wales as it once did, but its influence can still be seen across the region's landscape, architecture and communities. When the museum eventually reopens, visitors will find some new facilities, but the purpose of the place will remain much the same: to tell the story of the workers, their craft and an industry that helped shape an entire region. The additional funding is therefore not just an investment in a museum, but in keeping that history accessible to generations who may otherwise know little about it.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas mother with Alzheimer's left her home to her daughter in a 2007 will, but her son used a power of attorney to deed himself a share for $10; an appeals court ruled the transfer invalid
articles.summary: A family dispute over a Texas woman's home has ended with an appeals court upholding a ruling that invalidated a property transfer made by her son using a
articles.body: A family dispute over a Texas woman's home has ended with an appeals court upholding a ruling that invalidated a property transfer made by her son using a power of attorney. The mother, Betty Lou Casey, had left her Arlington residence to her daughter in a 2007 will. Years later, her son, Danny Prine, used a power of attorney purportedly granted by his mother to transfer the property to himself and her for a stated consideration of just $10. In an opinion filed on November 19, 2026, available on Justia, the Texas Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's decision, finding that Casey lacked the mental capacity to execute the power of attorney on which the transfer depended.A 2007 will left the Arlington home to the daughterCasey had three children: Sheila Fisher, Danny Prine and Sherry Neustupa. Her will, dated August 7, 2007, named Fisher as the independent executor of her estate and specifically left her Tarrant County residence on Milby Road in Arlington to her. The remainder of her estate was to be divided equally among the three children.Casey had also signed a durable power of attorney in 2007, naming Fisher as her agent. However, on November 21, 2014, she executed another power of attorney that designated Prine as her agent and Sherry as the alternative agent. Casey had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2014. Her condition gradually deteriorated, and she died on November 13, 2021, aged 92.During the probate process, Fisher discovered that her brother had executed a warranty deed on February 5, 2021, using the 2014 power of attorney. The document purported to convey the Arlington property to Prine and Casey as joint tenants for a stated consideration of $10. The deed did not contain survivorship language. Prine later re-recorded the deed on July 14, 2022, after Fisher had demanded that he leave the property.Medical evidence raised questions about the power of attorneyFisher challenged the validity of the 2014 power of attorney and the subsequent property deed. She argued that their mother did not have the mental capacity to execute the document that authorised Prine to act on her behalf. During the trial, Casey's treating physician, Dr Joe Perryman III, testified that he had treated her from 2013 to 2020. She had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and dementia in 2014 and was prescribed medications for cognitive decline. Her primary symptom was memory loss, and her condition progressively worsened.Casey's grandson also testified that he had noticed her memory problems as early as 2011. By 2014, she was increasingly confused, sometimes unable to remember what had happened the previous day, and could no longer manage her finances or prepare meals independently. Fisher described similar changes, saying their mother frequently forgot to pay bills, misplaced belongings and sometimes forgot to eat. She had also begun helping Casey with meals, shopping and medical appointments.An important part of the evidence came from Prine himself. On November 21, 2014, the same day Casey signed the power of attorney naming him as her agent, he had submitted a sworn statement in another estate matter describing his mother as incapacitated because of dementia and unable to manage her affairs. Although Prine later testified that Casey appeared lucid when she signed the document, the probate court found that she lacked the necessary mental capacity.Appeals court upholds the invalidation of the deedThe probate court ruled on March 6, 2025, that the 2014 power of attorney was invalid, the February 2021 deed was invalid, and full ownership of the Arlington property vested in Fisher immediately upon Casey's death. Prine challenged the decision, arguing that the evidence did not establish his mother's incapacity and that the court had wrongly invalidated the deed. He also raised complaints about his sister's handling of the estate.The appeals court rejected his arguments. It explained that the evidence was sufficient to support the finding that Casey did not understand the nature and consequences of signing the 2014 power of attorney. It also noted that Prine's own sworn statement about her incapacity, made on the very day she signed the document, supported that conclusion.The court further explained that a transaction in which an agent transfers property to himself is presumed unfair under the applicable fiduciary principles, placing the burden on the agent to demonstrate that it was fair. Because Prine's authority rested on a power of attorney executed when Casey lacked the required mental capacity, the subsequent deed was voidable. The court found that Fisher had filed the action within the applicable four-year limitation period. On November 19, 2026, the Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's judgment, leaving Fisher with full ownership of the Milby Road property under her mother's will.You use AI every day. articles.title: A West Sussex couple won £1 million on EuroMillions after their 12-week-old son underwent five-hour surgery for a cleft lip and palate; they now plan a Disneyland Paris trip with their two children
articles.summary: A West Sussex couple won £1 million on the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw. The win came after months of worry over their baby son’s health.
articles.body: A West Sussex couple won £1 million on the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw. The win came after months of worry over their baby son’s health. Matt Cole and his fiancée Courtney Cockerton discovered the win after their son Rupert underwent a five-hour operation to repair a cleft lip and palate when he was just 12 weeks old. The family had known before his birth that he would need surgery, but his parents said they were unprepared for the experience.According to the Sussex World, the couple plan to take Rupert and their two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Ivy, to Disneyland Paris. They also hope to use the winnings to buy a new home and car and provide greater security for their young family.How months of concern over couple’s baby’s health ended with a £1 million winMatt and Courtney had known before Rupert was born that he would need an operation to repair his cleft lip and palate. The procedure took place when he was 12 weeks old and lasted five hours. He also had to stay in hospital overnight. Matt said that knowing about the surgery in advance had not prepared them for seeing their baby go through it at such a young age. The family had faced difficult months around Rupert’s treatment.Matt said, “We’ve been incredibly fortunate that Rupert fed so well when he was born, as cleft conditions can often make feeding difficult. The support we’ve received from NHS staff has been amazing and we’re so grateful for everything they’ve done for us.”The £1 million win turned the couple’s Disneyland Paris dream into a family planThe £1 million win had allowed the couple to plan a trip they had long wanted to take with their children. Matt and Courtney hoped to travel to Disneyland Paris with five-month-old Rupert and their two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Ivy. They planned to take the Eurostar from St Pancras International Station to Paris Gare du Nord.The journey would be different from their recent trips to London, which had been for Rupert’s medical appointments at Evelina London Children’s Hospital. Courtney said, “We’ve always dreamt of taking her to Disneyland Paris and seeing her face light up when she meets her favourite characters. Now, thanks to this incredible win, that’s the first thing on our list.”How the lottery win brought relief after months of family health worriesCourtney said Rupert’s medical experience had affected the whole family. She also praised Ivy for the way she had responded as the big sister while her younger brother went through treatment.Although Ivy was only two-and-a-half, Courtney said she had been brilliant and had taken everything in her stride. She described her daughter as caring towards Rupert.The couple’s planned visit to Disneyland Paris was intended to create special memories together after the difficult months. Matt said, “Our family and friends have been just as shocked as we are about the win, but they’re absolutely over the moon for us. After everything we’ve been through recently, it feels like we’ve had a really lucky break.”The couple planned to buy a new home and car with their lottery winningsAlongside the Disneyland Paris holiday, Matt and Courtney planned to use their winnings to buy a new home and a new car. The win was expected to give their young family greater security.Matt said, “Through everything that has been happening, I still managed to find time to buy a EuroMillions Lucky Dip ticket. I’m so glad I did – I could never have imagined what would happen next.”“When I realised I’d won £1 million, I genuinely couldn’t believe it. I checked it over and over again. Even now it still hasn’t properly sunk in.”Every EuroMillions entry receives a unique UK Millionaire Maker code, made up of four letters and five numbers. The code is automatically entered into the UK Millionaire Maker draw, held on the same days as the EuroMillions draw.Disclaimer: This article is based on information reported by the Sussex World about Matt Cole and Courtney Cockerton’s £1 million EuroMillions win and their son Rupert’s medical treatment. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the family’s experiences or the lottery win.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Italian blacksmith spent more than 50 years building a forest amusement park with 37 handmade rides that run without electricity and are free for visitors
articles.summary: For more than 50 years, Bruno Ferrin from Italy has been turning a patch of woodland near Treviso into an unusual amusement park filled with handmade
articles.body: For more than 50 years, Bruno Ferrin from Italy has been turning a patch of woodland near Treviso into an unusual amusement park filled with handmade rides powered by people and physics rather than conventional electric motors. What began in 1968 as an attempt to run a small food stand on Montello hill gradually grew into Ai Pioppi, a free amusement park containing 37 attractions. Ferrin built the rides himself, often using old steel tubes and discarded materials, despite having no formal training in engineering or physics. The result is an eccentric playground where bicycles, ropes, weights and mechanical forces provide the power.How Bruno Ferrin built ‘Osteria Ai Pioppi’ amusement park despite having no formal training in engineering or physicsFerrin first arrived at the poplar forest on Montello hill near Treviso in 1968, looking for a way to earn money during his spare time. He and his wife, Marisa, established a food and wine stand called Osteria Ai Pioppi, or Tavern at the Poplars, beside a country road near the Piave River.According to Atlas Obscura, the first ride appeared almost by accident. Ferrin wanted to install a swing to attract families but needed two hooks. A local blacksmith told him he could use a welding machine and make them himself. After spending three hours learning to weld, Ferrin returned with the hooks and discovered that he enjoyed creating things from metal.A slide followed, then rocking horses and more attractions. Ferrin soon realised that visitors were coming to the property as much for the rides as for the food. Instead of following a formal business plan, he kept designing and building new attractions one after another. More than 50 years later, the amusement park covers roughly 65,000 square feet of woodland.As per Aipioppi’s official site, Ferrin says, “My life has been intense. With age, strength wanes, but enthusiasm remains that of the first day. For a few years I have been working with my nephew Francesco. We design, build, maintain.”Ferrin, who was born in Treviso in 1937, left compulsory schooling at the age of 10 and worked in several jobs before becoming involved with the restaurant. Although he never had any formal training, he based his craft purely on observation and intuition, which he says he progressively honed.Ai Pioppi's handmade rides use human power and mechanical physicsUnlike conventional amusement parks, Ai Pioppi does not rely on electric motors to operate its attractions. All 37 rides use human effort and mechanical principles to create movement.One of the most striking examples is a 12-foot-high cylindrical centrifuge made from colourful steel tubes. Four people sit at pedalling stations and generate the force needed to rotate the structure. As it spins faster, riders can be pushed against the inside wall by centrifugal force.Ferrin's designs often draw on things he encountered in everyday life. One attraction uses a rope and a weight to lift riders towards the forest canopy, inspired by his childhood experiences helping to swing the enormous bells of a local church. Another ride was inspired by the centrifuge forces he learned about from a television report on Cape Canaveral and astronaut training.The park includes attractions ranging from a 56-foot slide to a 55-ton pendulum. Ferrin works on the rides in his workshop, welding, drilling and painting components. Some projects take weeks, while others can take months or longer depending on what else needs his attention.Why Ferrin's electricity-free amusement park remains free to visitorsFerrin has continued to operate Ai Pioppi according to a philosophy that separates it from conventional commercial amusement parks. The rides are free, with income from the adjoining Osteria Ai Pioppi helping to keep the attraction open without an admission charge.Ferrin has reportedly rejected suggestions from friends that he should introduce even a small entrance fee. His approach is to let visitors eat at the restaurant, enjoy the surrounding forest and then use the rides without paying separately for them.The restaurant itself has become a substantial operation. It can accommodate up to 1,500 diners, while the park and restaurant operate on a seasonal schedule. The site is generally closed during the winter, reopens around late March on weekends and operates daily during August.The park's popularity has grown far beyond the local area. Visitors from Germany and Austria have travelled to Ai Pioppi, while a documentary broadcast on German television helped attract more German-speaking visitors. After the pandemic shutdown, Ferrin's family was reportedly overwhelmed by messages from customers asking when the restaurant and park would reopen.The forest itself is part of Ferrin's unusual amusement park designAi Pioppi is not simply a collection of rides placed inside a forest. Ferrin deliberately works around the existing landscape, sometimes allowing vegetation to grow around the attractions. Wisteria, for example, has enveloped part of a slide's supporting structure.Ferrin told Atlas Obscura that he tries to avoid interfering with plants when positioning a new ride. If a root is in the way, he considers the problem before deciding whether it should be cut. The surrounding landscape also has a significant history: the area near the Piave was part of the frontline between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces during the First World War, and Ferrin has occasionally encountered remnants of the conflict while digging.Safety is handled separately from Ferrin's informal approach to construction. Although he has no formal physics or engineering qualifications, each attraction is checked by a government-approved engineer, according to the Atlas Obscura report.Bruno Ferrin still builds new rides after more than five decadesFerrin has continued spending several hours a day in his workshop, developing new ideas and maintaining the existing attractions. His approach remains deliberately low-tech, with old steel tubes and other reused materials becoming components of new rides.He has also passed some of his knowledge to his grandson Francesco, who has been involved with the park for decades. Francesco now helps with its digital presence while learning the craft from his grandfather.Ferrin, who was 85, in 2022 when Atlas Obscura visited Ai Pioppi, had no plans to stop building rides. The amusement park that began with a food stand and a pair of handmade swing hooks had become a sprawling collection of mechanical attractions hidden among the trees near Treviso.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bay Area homeowners replacing broken gas furnaces from 2029 may face about $12,500 in additional costs under new emissions rules, with a new analysis finding electric heat-pump installations substantially more expensive
articles.summary: Homeowners across California’s Bay Area could face a significantly higher bill when replacing their natural gas heating systems under an upcoming
articles.body: Homeowners across California’s Bay Area could face a significantly higher bill when replacing their natural gas heating systems under an upcoming emissions regulation. A new assessment by the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and detailed in the district’s November 2026 implementation report, estimates that switching from a conventional gas furnace to an electric heat-pump system could add approximately $12,526 to installation costs for a typical single-family home. The requirement is part of Regulation 9, Rule 4, which aims to eliminate nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from newly installed natural gas-fired furnaces. The pollutant contributes to ground-level ozone and particulate pollution, both of which can affect public health and regional air quality. Under the current timeline, the zero-emissions standard will apply to covered furnaces from January 1, 2029. The regulation does not require homeowners to remove existing operational gas furnaces. Instead, it restricts the sale and installation of newly manufactured gas-fired equipment that does not meet the emissions standard, meaning households replacing their systems after the deadline will need to consider compliant alternatives.Heat pumps could significantly increase upfront expensesThe district’s cost assessment highlights the financial difference between conventional heating systems and electric alternatives. Installing a standard natural gas furnace in a single-family home is estimated to cost approximately $8,064, compared with around $20,590 for an electric heat-pump heating and cooling system.This creates an estimated upfront difference of $12,526. However, the financial comparison changes when homeowners also factor in air-conditioning expenses. Since heat pumps provide both heating and cooling, households that would otherwise purchase a separate central air-conditioning system could see the additional cost fall to approximately $2,095. The distinction is particularly relevant in the Bay Area, where an estimated 60% of homes already have central air conditioning. Existing electrical infrastructure and available space for outdoor equipment could also make certain installations less expensive.Electrical upgrades remain a concernWhile heat pumps are expected to offer long-term savings on energy bills, the initial installation could become more complicated for properties requiring electrical upgrades. According to the Air District’s assessment, electrical panel and service upgrades can cost several thousand dollars and, in particularly difficult cases, exceed $20,000. Around 3% of single-family homes and 10% of multifamily properties in California are estimated to have electrical panels that may require upgrades for full electrification.Infrastructure limitations could also affect installation timelines. Data cited in the report indicate that utility service upgrades can take more than 300 days for single-family homes and over 500 days for multifamily buildings. The transition could create additional challenges for apartment owners and tenants, particularly in older buildings where electrical capacity is limited. The district has also identified the possibility of landlords passing some improvement expenses on to renters.Homeowners could save on energy billsDespite the higher upfront investment, electric heat pumps could reduce household energy expenses over time. A study covering three Bay Area climate zones found that households installing minimum-efficiency heat pumps could save between $167 and $474 in their first year. More efficient variable-capacity systems could generate annual savings of approximately $364 to $733, depending on the property and existing equipment.However, the actual savings will vary according to electricity rates, household energy consumption and whether a property already has air conditioning. The availability of financial assistance is another consideration. The Air District’s November assessment noted that federal incentives for residential heat pumps have declined, while state rebates through the TECH Clean California programme were fully subscribed as of September 2026. Several local programmes continue to offer incentives generally ranging from $1,000 to $3,000.Changes to the regulation are still possibleThe 2029 deadline is not entirely settled. The Bay Area Air District has been examining implementation challenges through a working group involving more than 40 stakeholders, including housing representatives, technical experts, manufacturers and government agencies. District staff are scheduled to present their findings to the Board of Directors on December 2, 2026. Potential changes could address properties requiring extensive electrical work, buildings without existing air-conditioning systems and situations where installation costs are particularly difficult to manage. The furnace regulation follows a separate requirement covering residential water heaters. Under the revised timeline, smaller natural gas water heaters will face zero-NOx requirements from January 1, 2028, potentially requiring another round of equipment replacements for affected households.Reducing pollution from residential and commercial buildings is the main goal, but the most recent cost assessment emphasizes the potential infrastructure and financial difficulties.You use AI every day. articles.title: Toddlers remains found in Nabarangpur forest after 20-hour search
articles.summary: Two-year-old girl’s remains found in Nabarangpur forest after 20-hour search; wild animal suspected, forest teams monitor area near Udanti-Sitanadi.
articles.body: Koraput: Remains of a two-year-old girl, who went missing after allegedly being carried away by a wild animal, were recovered from a forest near her house in Nabarangpur district on Tuesday, following an extensive 20-hour search operation.The incident took place at Chadiyapada village under Raighar forest range. The child’s remains were found scattered in a forest nearly 1 km from her house, sending shockwaves through the village.Sources said the girl went missing around 8 pm on Monday, when she was allegedly picked up by a wild animal. She was reportedly lying on the verandah of her house while her father, Bishnu Gond, and other family members were having dinner inside. When the family realised that the child was missing, they launched a search with the help of villagers and informed the forest department.Forest personnel immediately launched a search operation and deployed the district police dog squad to trace the child. The dog squad eventually led the search teams to the spot where the remains were found.“The child’s remains were found inside the forest, around 1 km from her house. Her head, two legs and hands were found separated and scattered at the spot. The dog squad led our team to the location,” said Subhash Khuntia, assistant conservator of forests (ACF), Nabarangpur forest division.Khuntia said the exact animal responsible for the attack was yet to be ascertained. “It could be a leopard or a hyena. Though we do not have any known leopard population in the district, the incident site is close to Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve in neighbouring Chhattisgarh. There is a possibility of a leopard straying into our area,” he said.“At least three forest department teams are camping in the area to monitor the situation and track the animal’s movement. Villagers are also being sensitised about precautionary measures to avoid further attacks,” Khuntia added.The toddler was the second daughter of Bishnu Gond.
